subQuestions.questionText:
Various options are provided as possible answers. Choose the answer and write only the letter (A–D) next to the question number.

An example of chronic stress:
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D — Constant anxiety about meeting the expectations of others. (1)

Chronic stress is ongoing, constant and long-term. The other options describe once-off or situational tension (planning an event, a presentation, a disagreement) rather than a persistent state.

options.A: Always being tense about planning an upcoming event
options.B: Regularly feeling nervous before an important presentation
options.C: Frequent tension during a disagreement with friends
options.D: Constant anxiety about meeting the expectations of others

subQuestions.questionText: An example of an environmental intervention programme:
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C — A campaign to empower communities on the benefits of recycling waste efficiently. (1)

An environmental intervention programme actively involves the community in protecting or improving the environment (e.g. recycling). The other options deal with reporting crime, teaching sewage management, or research only.

options.A: Educational activities encouraging residents to report gang-related crimes in the area
options.B: A training course teaching the community how to effectively manage the sewage systems
options.C: A campaign to empower communities on the benefits of recycling waste efficiently
options.D: Research conducted by local authorities to highlight the effects of waste dumping in rivers

subQuestions.questionText: A social media footprint is the ...
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B — content a person shares and interacts with on social media that shapes their online identity. (1)

A social media (digital) footprint is the trail of content a person posts, likes and shares, which builds their online identity and reputation.

options.A: ability to stay completely anonymous while engaging frequently on social media platforms.
options.B: content a person shares and interacts with on social media that shapes their online identity.
options.C: number of followers an individual has on social media, irrespective of their online presence.
options.D: total number of social media platforms individuals join to send direct messages to others.

subQuestions.questionText: The National Qualifications Framework (NQF) provides a system ...
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C — that records the credits of each level of learning. (1)

The NQF is a system that registers and records qualifications and the credits attached to each of its levels.

options.A: of accreditation for approved educational institutions.
options.B: to standardise the curriculum across all training programmes.
options.C: that records the credits of each level of learning.
options.D: to enhance funding for higher education qualifications.

subQuestions.questionText: The difference between indigenous games and traditional sports is that indigenous games ...
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A — focus on recreation, while traditional sports focus on standard rules. (1)

Indigenous games are informal and recreational, whereas traditional sports are governed by set/standard rules.

options.A: focus on recreation, while traditional sports focus on standard rules.
options.B: are played by children, while traditional sports are played by adults.
options.C: use elaborate kits, while traditional sports require basic equipment.
options.D: are the same globally, while traditional sports differ across cultures.

subQuestions.questionText:
Give ONE word/term for the following description. Write only the word/term.

A South African law that helps disadvantaged groups, people with disabilities and racial minorities to get better job opportunities.
subQuestions.memoText:
Employment Equity Act (EEA), 1998 (Act 55 of 1998). (1)

'Employment Equity Act' / 'EEA' is accepted.
subQuestions.topic: The world of work and human rights

subQuestions.questionText:
Give ONE word/term for the following description. Write only the word/term.

The ability to understand what another person is feeling and to see things from their point of view.

subQuestions.questionText:
Give ONE word/term for the following description. Write only the word/term.

A collection of documents, achievements, skills and certifications that shows an individual's professional abilities and experiences.
subQuestions.memoText: Career portfolio / portfolio / professional portfolio. (1)

subQuestions.questionText:
Answer in full sentences.

Define the term cardiovascular endurance as used in physical education.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. Any ONE of:
• The ability of the body to maintain a moderate to high level of physical activity for an extended period, without experiencing significant drops in physical performance.
• The ability of the heart/lungs/circulatory system to sufficiently deliver oxygen to the muscles during prolonged exercise, enabling the body to sustain physical activity without excessive fatigue.
• The ability of the body to recover quickly after exertion, efficiently restoring normal heart rate/oxygen levels after exercise.
(1 x 2) (2)

subQuestions.questionText:
Answer in full sentences.

What is expected of you when answering a 'critically discuss' question in an assessment task?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. Any ONE of:
• Explore various opinions/arguments on the topic, evaluating their advantages/disadvantages for a well-rounded discussion.
• Provide relevant examples/studies/data to support your arguments, showing a thorough understanding of the topic.
• Think about the potential effects/consequences of the issue, considering immediate and long-term impacts.
• Offer a reasoned judgement based on your analysis, keeping personal biases aside.

subQuestions.questionText:
Answer in full sentences.

Discuss the importance of reading the questions carefully during an examination.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. Any ONE of:
• It helps you get an overview of the areas/content covered, so you can identify which questions are easier to answer first.
• It helps you identify/underline action verbs, so you respond only to what is expected and avoid wasting time on incorrect answers or misinterpreting the question.
• It helps you determine and understand exactly what is being asked and process the instructions clearly, making you feel less stressed and more confident and in control of your answers.
• It helps you identify key words/main points/phrases, which guide your responses and ensure you answer on the correct topic.
• It helps you notice if there is more than one part or sub-question, so you do not miss out on any question.
• It helps you answer in full and according to the mark allocations, improving academic performance and maximising marks.
• It helps you judge how long your answer should be and how many points to give, so you manage time effectively.
(1 x 2) (2)

subQuestions.passageText:
TAX OBLIGATION: A CHALLENGE IN SOUTH AFRICA

Tax fraud often sparks a debate about fairness and responsibility among citizens. Entrepreneurs face challenges in balancing their business growth while meeting their tax obligations. However, having tax-paying citizens is still vital to South Africa.

[Adapted from www.businesstech.co.za. Accessed on 7 January 2025.]
subQuestions.questionText:
Study the text above and answer the question. Write your answers in full sentences.

Give TWO reasons why it is considered an act of fraud if citizens are not paying taxes.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award ONE mark for each response. Any TWO of:
• It violates the legal duty of individuals/businesses to contribute to public funds.
• It deprives the government of essential revenue used for national development/services.
• It creates a financial burden on tax-paying citizens, who may pay higher amounts to cover the shortfall.
• It involves knowingly/deliberately misrepresenting financial details.
• It includes concealing income/falsifying financial statements/using offshore accounts/setting up shell companies to hide assets/avoiding tax obligations.
(2 x 1) (2)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain how entrepreneurs can effectively manage the tax obligations of their businesses.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. Any ONE of:
• Keep detailed financial records/conduct audits to ensure accurate tax reporting and prevent errors.
• Budget for tax deductions so they comply with payments and avoid penalties.
• Separate business and personal accounts, which simplifies tax filing and improves financial transparency.
• Set aside income/make estimated tax payments, thereby preventing financial strain.
• Claim deductions on business expenses/charitable giving, thus reducing taxable income and overall tax liability.
• Choose the right business structure/plan to optimise tax benefits and minimise liabilities.
• Hire an affordable tax expert/practitioner/accountant to assist with submissions, compliance and reducing financial risks.
• Enrol for a business course/training/educate themselves on tax responsibilities, so they learn how to manage taxes effectively.
(1 x 2) (2)

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss how having responsible tax-paying citizens could benefit the country.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. Any ONE of:
• Provides enough funds to develop infrastructure/healthcare/education/transport/security, promoting economic sustainability.
• Means less money is borrowed from other countries, resulting in lower national debt and financial stability.
• Funds social programmes that support the poor, reducing income inequality and improving living standards.
• Provides finances for public services such as the military/law enforcement/emergency services, thereby protecting citizens and maintaining order.
• Maintains good infrastructure/economic stability and creates better job opportunities, attracting businesses and investors.
• Builds a sense of duty in the country, allowing citizens to contribute to national progress and growth.
• Improves the financial image of the country, which may attract international trade, investment and global partnerships.
• Improves the country's credit rating, enabling access to loans/investment at lower interest rates.
• Enhances the ability to respond to crises/disasters through readily available public funds.
(1 x 2) (2)

questions.title: SECTION B (Compulsory) — Question 2: Human Rights Violations (Safe and healthy living)
questions.passageText:
HUMAN RIGHTS VIOLATIONS — Safe and healthy living

The recent sale of contaminated food products by some small businesses in communities raised serious concerns about public health, consumer protection and human rights. Media reports indicated that some businesses had been selling hazardous food products, impacting on safe and healthy living conditions in communities. Investigations revealed that many of these businesses were operating illegally, failing to comply with food safety regulations, thereby putting the community's health at serious risk.

Although some of these businesses are owned by foreign nationals, the real issue is not about nationality, but rather the lack of enforcement of food safety laws and non-compliance by certain businesses. However, some of these owners who have been accused of selling contaminated products have become victims of xenophobia in their communities, impacting on their mental well-being. The Bill of Rights protects individuals against discrimination and guarantees the rights of all individuals, regardless of their nationality. These public health and safety standards must align with human rights to protect consumers from harm. Addressing this crisis requires a collaborative effort from individuals, communities and the government.

Glossary: contaminated — unsafe or harmful for human consumption/use.

[Adapted from www.pmg.org.za. Accessed on 2 March 2025.]

subQuestions.questionText: State how being exposed to contaminated food products may impact a person's right to healthy living.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award ONE mark for each response. Any TWO of:
• Takes away their right to safe/healthy living and makes day-to-day living more challenging.
• Increases the likelihood of exposure to foodborne illnesses/food poisoning/infections.
• Leads to long-term/serious physical health issues such as cancer/organ damage/metabolic disorders/possible death.
• Could mean that the nutrients needed to stay healthy and nourished are absent.
• May cause malnutrition/developmental issues in children.
• Increases the need for medical care.
• Makes the elderly and those with pre-existing conditions more vulnerable to further health complications.
• Weakens a person's immune system.
(2 x 1) (2)
subQuestions.topic: Human rights violations: safe and healthy living

subQuestions.questionText: Describe ONE possible benefit of small businesses in communities.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. Any ONE of:
• Creates job opportunities/labour absorption, since local community members supply products or are employed by them.
• Serves a diverse group of people at affordable costs, as they are conveniently located within communities.
• Promotes employment/entrepreneurship, which lowers dependency on social grants/government support, alleviates poverty and reduces the crime rate.
• Provides basic needs to the community, making them more accessible and improving the standard of living.
• Funds charity organisations, reducing the load on government-funded programmes.
• Supplies in-demand/alternative products, which boosts local revenue.
• Partners with other local businesses, increasing business opportunities/unity/skills development in the community.
• Supports overall economic growth by paying taxes to government.
• Promotes cultural diversity by offering traditional/locally crafted goods unique to the community.
(1 x 2) (2)
subQuestions.topic: Human rights violations: safe and healthy living

subQuestions.questionText: Explain ONE factor that could increase xenophobic attitudes towards foreign business owners within communities.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. Any ONE of:
• A lack of education/awareness about diversity and inclusion, resulting in ignorance about newcomers in the area.
• The spreading of fake news/rumours/gossip about immigrants, increasing fear and suspicion of people from other countries.
• Resentment towards foreigners when the economy is bad, as locals may believe they steal job opportunities from citizens.
• A history of conflict where people hold onto prejudices about foreigners and pass them down through generations.
• Biased media reporting that blames foreigners for crime/unemployment in the community or country.
• Cultural/language/religious differences between locals and foreigners, so locals feel foreign nationals do not integrate with or understand them.
• People in power or trusted figures spreading propaganda, leading others to adopt the same beliefs to fit in or avoid conflict.
• Sensationalised news reports chasing clicks/views, reinforcing negative stereotypes and discrimination.
• The spreading of myths about foreign nationals, causing people to believe and support them without evidence.
• Foreign business owners who do not comply with local food safety requirements, causing anger in communities.
• Competition over limited housing/resources, which fuels jealousy towards foreign nationals.
• Government failures in service delivery, leading locals to wrongly blame foreigners for their struggles.
(1 x 2) (2)
subQuestions.topic: Human rights violations: safe and healthy living

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss the possible impact of discrimination on the mental well-being of victims of xenophobia.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks each for TWO well-explained responses. Any TWO of:
• Feelings of inferiority/unworthiness/not being good enough, resulting in low self-esteem, self-doubt and diminished self-worth.
• Constant worry/fear of being treated unfairly, causing increased anxiety and stress.
• Sadness and a loss of interest in activities, leading to depression and hopelessness.
• Emotional distress and interpersonal conflict, causing heightened anger/frustration and a desire for revenge.
• Loneliness, so they may isolate or exclude themselves from social situations.
• Reduced productivity and personal drive, causing them to disengage from daily activities and lose motivation.
• Difficulty dealing with victimisation, resulting in emotional pain, suicidal thoughts, unhealthy coping mechanisms or risky behaviour.
(2 x 2) (4)
subQuestions.topic: Human rights violations: safe and healthy living

subQuestions.questionText: Assess the responsibility of the media in creating awareness on safe and healthy living.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks each for TWO well-explained responses. Any TWO of:
• The media should expose failures to render services, ensuring people are aware of issues that threaten their right to safe and healthy living.
• Media investigations should draw attention to environmental hazards, as these directly affect public health.
• Reporters must base stories on verified facts/evidence, emphasising the struggles of communities living in unsafe conditions.
• The media should give a platform to individuals affected by poor sanitation/hazardous workplaces, putting pressure on authorities to act.
• Journalists should use television/newspapers/online platforms to report on the impact of poor living conditions, educating a wider audience about human health.
• Exposing false information about harmful chemicals/pollutants, pushing for stricter regulations to protect public well-being.
• The media should collaborate with advocacy groups/activists demanding clean air, safe drinking water and improved sanitation.
• Giving more coverage to unsafe living conditions helps expose negligence and corruption.
• Sharing real stories from people in unsafe environments drives action and policy reform and makes government accountable.
• Educating society through documentaries/in-depth reports about toxic waste/untreated sewage/global warming, mobilising communities against illegal dumping.
• Analysing and critiquing government policies affecting access to clean water and air, highlighting positive initiatives.
• Highlighting success stories of safe-living initiatives to encourage communities to adopt positive practices.
• Providing multilingual health information so diverse communities understand the risks and solutions.
(2 x 2) (4)
subQuestions.topic: Human rights violations: safe and healthy living

subQuestions.questionText: Recommend TWO ways in which the government could reinforce current laws that prevent the sale of contaminated goods. In EACH answer, also indicate how this can ensure safe and healthy living within communities.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award THREE marks each for TWO well-explained responses (recommendation + how it works + link to safe and healthy living). Any TWO of:
• Impose heavier punishments, pressuring businesses to follow food safety regulations and deterring bad practice, which reduces the amount of contaminated goods sold in communities.
• Collaborate more effectively with local municipalities, so food safety violations are caught and addressed quickly at community level, enhancing public health through compliance with national standards.
• Ensure law enforcement/local government do regular/random inspections at stores; surprise visits make businesses more likely to comply, reducing the storage of unsafe products.
• Address consumer complaints about unhealthy food through local/community platforms, so unsafe products are recalled and non-compliant businesses are fined.
• Provide more resources to agencies that monitor safety, giving them the capacity to ensure manufacturers and sellers follow the law, reducing the sale of contaminated food.
• Reduce administrative backlogs in courts, so cases are dealt with speedily, holding businesses accountable timeously for harmful practices.
• Reinforce regulatory bodies that enforce national food safety standards by certifying/testing/investigating products, reducing the risk of dangerous products being consumed.
• Run public awareness campaigns/education programmes to prompt individuals to report unsafe businesses, empowering them to take responsibility for their own food safety.
• Update reporting platforms to make them more user-friendly, so consumers can report violations easily, ensuring businesses supply safe products.
• Review laws to make them more specific, preventing consumers from being misled into buying poor-quality goods and phasing out the sale of unsafe products.
(2 x 3) (6) [20]
subQuestions.topic: Human rights violations: safe and healthy living

questions.title: SECTION B (Compulsory) — Question 3: Human factors causing ill health (Smoking in adolescents)
questions.passageText:
HUMAN FACTORS CAUSING ILL HEALTH — Smoking in adolescents

Factors contributing to ill health can negatively impact an individual's health and future opportunities. Recent media reports indicate high incidences of learners smoking in schools, probably due to easy access to cigarettes and vapes. The normalisation of smoking among young people has led to a rise in experimentation and addiction, affecting their health and academic performance.

Social media plays a significant role in influencing the lifestyle choices of the youth today. Poor habits and choices made early in life could have lasting effects on the overall long-term well-being and quality of life of individuals.

A focused approach to personal well-being can help individuals make informed choices and avoid harmful substances. Schools play an essential role in guiding learners towards positive habits by implementing effective measures. These measures could empower learners to make informed decisions that benefit their long-term health and future growth.

Glossary: vapes — electronic cigarettes.

[Adapted from www.pmc.ncbi.co.za. Accessed on 3 January 2025.]

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term human factors causing ill health.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. Any ONE of:
• Behaviours/decisions made by individuals or groups that may negatively impact their physical or mental health.
• Social influences that lead to unhealthy choices, which may result in disease or poor health outcomes.
• Lifestyle choices or societal pressures that contribute to the deterioration of a person's well-being.
• Personal actions or habits that increase vulnerability to sickness or health conditions.
• Cultural practices of individuals or communities that may lead to the development of diseases or poor health.
(1 x 2) (2)

subQuestions.questionText: Describe ONE potential long-term health risk for young smokers.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. Any ONE of:
• Developing several types of cancer, leading to death due to the seriousness of the disease.
• Damage to the cardiovascular system, increasing the risk of heart disease/heart attacks/strokes.
• Reduced mineral/vitamin absorption, which may result in weaker bones/fractures/a weakened immune system.
• Poor mental health/cognitive decline/dementia/chronic respiratory diseases (bronchitis/asthma/TB/pneumonia), resulting in a poor quality of life.
• Eye problems/loss of vision, which impacts negatively on daily life.
• Poor reproductive health in men and women, which may lead to infertility/miscarriage/stillbirth/sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).
• Damage to the teeth/gums/supporting tissues, causing chronic gum disease and permanent tooth loss.
• Interference with the growth process, potentially leading to stunted growth in height or overall development.
(1 x 2) (2)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why learners who smoke are more likely to experiment with other substances.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks for a well-explained response. Any ONE of:
• They use smoking to relieve stress, making them more willing to try stronger substances for better relief.
• They are addicted to nicotine or no longer get the desired effect, so they seek stronger experiences by trying other substances.
• They are less anxious about trying other substances because they have already taken one risk, challenge norms or rebel against authority.
• They start associating with people who use other substances or succumb to peer pressure, increasing their chances of trying them.
• They become curious about other substances trending on social media and want to explore new experiences.
• They feel more grown-up/independent/mature, which drives them to try other 'adult' behaviours like drinking or using drugs.
• They struggle with mental health issues and try other substances in search of a more effective way to cope.
• They lack the finances to sustain their addiction and turn to cheaper alternatives to support their habit.
(1 x 2) (2)

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss TWO ways in which exposure to social media could promote the use of substances among the youth.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks each for TWO well-explained responses. Social media may:
• Portray 'using' as glamorous/desirable/normal, making it appealing to the youth.
• Depict 'using' as a normal part of social life, so the youth see it as acceptable behaviour.
• Downplay the risks associated with substance use, so the youth are unaware of the potential consequences.
• Influence teenagers' belief systems, suggesting substance use is necessary for social acceptance or to cope with stress.
• Encourage sensation-seeking behaviour, which could lead to risky behaviours.
• Create a platform for social learning (TikTok/Instagram/Snapchat), where the youth learn from and imitate these behaviours.
• Desensitise the youth to the consequences of substance use, making them more likely to engage in risky behaviour.
• Target vulnerable youth who are more susceptible to the content, making them more prone to peer pressure.
• Highlight substance use in movies/TV shows/music videos, which normalises it.
• Feature influencers/celebrities/role models who encourage unhealthy lifestyle choices, which younger followers copy.
(2 x 2) (4)

subQuestions.questionText: Recommend TWO measures that could be implemented by schools to discourage learners from smoking. Motivate EACH answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award TWO marks each for TWO well-explained responses (measure + motivation). Any TWO of:
• Display educational posters/signage around the school reinforcing anti-smoking messages, which act as constant reminders to avoid smoking.
• Invite guest speakers/health professionals to talk about the dangers of smoking; first-hand experiences leave a lasting impression on learners.
• Implement smoking prevention programmes/workshops that educate learners about the dangers of smoking and the rights of non-smokers.
• Encourage community service linked to anti-smoking campaigns, helping learners understand the impact of smoking on health.
• Make corrective programmes compulsory for learners caught smoking as part of the code of conduct, isolating them from outside influences.
• Host health projects/competitions focused on healthy living, increasing awareness of the benefits of a healthy lifestyle.
• Amend the code of conduct to impose fines/demerits/suspension for smoking, deterring learners who do not want the consequences.
• Revoke learner privileges, making them afraid of missing out on opportunities.
• Compel learners who smoke to attend counselling and communicate revised rules at parent meetings/assemblies.
• Promote recreational/sport activities to relieve stress, so learners do not use smoking as a coping mechanism.
• Conduct random searches to prevent learners bringing illegal substances to school and exposing others.
• Patrol smoking spots/install smoke detectors in bathrooms so smokers can be caught and disciplined.
(2 x 2) (4)

subQuestions.questionText: Assess the significance of a personal lifestyle plan in helping young people to avoid substance abuse. In EACH answer, also indicate how this plan may help them make better lifestyle choices.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award THREE marks each for TWO well-explained responses (significance + elaboration + link to better lifestyle choices). Any TWO of:
• It creates a sense of direction about the activities they engage in, guided by their life goals, resulting in wiser choices and preventing risky teenage activities.
• It encourages healthy habits such as regular exercise and a balanced diet, enhancing physical and mental well-being, so they are less likely to turn to substances.
• It equips individuals with tools like mindfulness and time management to handle stress and anxiety, helping them manage emotions and behaviour without substances.
• Setting and achieving goals grows self-esteem and confidence, so they are less inclined to use substances to cope with insecurities and instead prioritise mental and physical health.
• Clearly defined coping mechanisms teach them to handle difficult emotions through practices like meditation or mentorship, building emotional resilience.
• Identifying positive, supportive people builds a strong social support system that relieves the pressure to use substances.
• Structured routines enhance focus and discipline, helping them stay on track with studies and interests and resist temptation.
• Keeping a journal or doing creative activities provides alternative ways to manage challenges without resorting to substances.
• It provides mechanisms to make informed, thoughtful decisions, teaching them to weigh the pros and cons and consider consequences.
• It allows tracking of progress and achievements, giving a sense of accomplishment that reinforces self-efficacy and motivation to stay healthy.
• It promotes involvement in community/service activities, giving a sense of purpose and belonging that decreases the appeal of substance use.
(2 x 3) (6) [20]

questions.title: SECTION C (Answer any TWO of Questions 4, 5 and 6) — Question 4: Labour laws (Workers' rights and obligations in the workplace)
questions.passageText:
SECTION C: Answer any TWO questions in this section. Responses must be in paragraphs; marks are awarded only for responses written in full sentences. If all three questions are answered, only the first TWO are marked.

LABOUR LAWS — Workers' rights and obligations in the workplace

A recent investigation into South Africa's restaurant industry has revealed that some restaurants failed to comply with labour laws, and young workers were reluctant to report these violations. It was also found that some trade union members were implicated in unacceptable workplace behaviour.

[Adapted from www.actionsa.org. Accessed on 24 March 2025.]

Write paragraphs on labour laws using the three points below as a guideline.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly state FOUR ways in which employers could ensure that labour laws are successfully implemented within their organisations.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award ONE mark for each response. Any FOUR of:
• Provide clear, legally compliant employment contracts.
• Strictly follow health and safety regulations.
• Implement effective grievance procedures/a whistle-blower policy.
• Comply with legal limits on working hours/leave/fair wages/hiring practices/working conditions/compensation/overtime payment.
• Foster a mutually respectful, inclusive workplace environment.
• Effectively address workplace harassment/discrimination/bullying.
• Regularly conduct training/workshops/audits on workplace rights, anti-discrimination policies and fair employment practices.
• Provide employees with accessible resources and human resource (HR) support.
• Adhere to transparent, unbiased, equal-opportunity recruitment processes.
• Support employees who join trade unions.
• Encourage employee feedback on workplace practices.
• Consult legal experts/HR specialists for updates on changes in labour legislation to keep policies compliant.
(4 x 1) (4)

subQuestions.questionText: Analyse how inappropriate behaviour of some trade union members could have a negative impact on the work environment.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award FOUR marks each for TWO well-explained responses. For full marks a candidate must give a statement, elaborate on it, qualify it and give an outcome. Any TWO of:
• Participating in unauthorised/illegal strikes disrupts business operations and violates employment agreements, causing financial losses and increasing tension between workers and management.
• Harassing or intimidating non-union employees to force them to join the union creates a hostile work environment, fostering resentment, making colleagues feel unsafe and causing them to seek other employment.
• Spending excessive time organising meetings and distributing union materials instead of doing their jobs reduces productivity and affects the company's overall efficiency and reputation.
• Spreading false or misleading information about company policies or working conditions stirs discontent, creates unnecessary conflict and damages trust between workers and management.
• Denying non-union members access to certain benefits and isolating them from information they are entitled to, while favouring union members, leads to workplace discrimination and division.
• Refusing to follow workplace rules or being frequently absent, arguing they are protected by the union, makes it difficult for managers to enforce order, leading to an undisciplined, disorganised environment.
• Protecting underperforming or misbehaving union members despite their wrongdoing makes it difficult for management to enforce the rules and compromises disciplinary processes, leading to a dysfunctional workplace and poor work relationships.
• Creating divisions among staff, where union members favour each other over non-members, fosters resentment and low morale, reducing cooperation and teamwork and lowering productivity.
(2 x 4) (8)

subQuestions.questionText: Evaluate the impact on a young worker who reports labour law violations in the workplace.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award FOUR marks each for TWO well-explained responses. For full marks (evaluation) a candidate must give a POSITIVE statement and qualify it, then a NEGATIVE statement and qualify it. Any TWO of:
• They may face retaliation from colleagues/management and be labelled a troublemaker, be overlooked for promotion, lose their job or lose salary; but they may also feel pride and empowerment knowing they are standing up for their rights and those of their co-workers.
• They may experience increased stress and anxiety because they fear the repercussions; however, it could also give them a sense of relief, knowing they have taken the necessary steps to address injustice.
• They may have strained or damaged relationships with colleagues who see them as an informant; but they could also earn the respect of others who appreciate their courage and commitment to doing the right thing.
• They could receive legal protection, ensuring their safety against victimisation; while in other cases they may still face a lack of support from the union or intimidation from the employer, leaving them feeling powerless and discouraged from reporting further violations.
• It may bring positive change in the workplace through better enforcement of labour laws; but the process could take time, and the young worker may feel disillusioned if the issue is not addressed quickly.
• They may gain recognition for their integrity and professionalism, potentially advancing their career long term; although they may experience a temporary setback in promotion as some in the organisation see them as a troublemaker.
• They may feel vulnerable to continued scrutiny from management or other employees who disagree with their actions; however, they may also be raising awareness of workers' rights, empowering other employees to speak out.
(2 x 4) (8) [20]

questions.title: SECTION C (Answer any TWO of Questions 4, 5 and 6) — Question 5: The media (Being cyber-savvy)
questions.passageText:
THE MEDIA — Being cyber-savvy

In an advancing digital world, the use of electronic media is now rapidly replacing print media among young people. Hence, young people are becoming more cyber-savvy, developing online skills that may assist them in counteracting unemployment while learning to stay cyber safe at the same time.

[Adapted from www.scirp.org. Accessed on 24 March 2025.]

Write paragraphs on the media using the three points below as a guideline.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly state FOUR ways to maintain cyber safety while developing online skills to counteract unemployment.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award ONE mark for each response. Any FOUR of:
• Be cautious with links and attachments from unknown sources.
• Keep personal information private and secure.
• Be aware of online scams/phishing/hacking and other online threats.
• Protect your online reputation.
• Avoid joining online platforms that could result in malware/virus infections.
• Do not fall prey to demands for payment in exchange for job offers.
• Keep software and operating systems up to date to handle security vulnerabilities, and use reputable antivirus software.
• Monitor online accounts and credit reports for suspicious activity.
• Check the privacy settings on social media platforms regularly.
• Be cautious when using public computers or public Wi-Fi.
• Use encryption when sending personal information.
• Safeguard sensitive information such as passwords, bank card numbers and addresses.
(4 x 1) (4)

subQuestions.questionText: Analyse how being cyber-savvy could help young people to counteract unemployment.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award FOUR marks each for TWO well-explained responses. For full marks a candidate must give a statement, elaborate on it, qualify it and give an outcome. Any TWO of:
• Being in control of their digital footprint means they can ensure their online activity does not harm their image; because employers often research candidates, they are more inclined to employ people with a clean digital record.
• Effectively navigating online job platforms like LinkedIn and job boards opens up a competitive, global job market and lets them customise applications, helping them find opportunities more easily.
• Expanding their social and professional networks helps them connect with industry experts and gain access to job leads, improving their chances of finding employment.
• Understanding the relationship between brands, influencers and consumers, and being able to create content on TikTok/YouTube/Instagram, lets them grow their own audience and opens a pathway to income from companies seeking influential people to promote their brand.
• Acquiring digital skills for emerging roles by keeping up with the latest tools and trends gives them skills in high-demand sectors like technology, digital marketing and e-commerce, opening new career avenues.
• Using online learning platforms and free or paid courses lets them enhance their skills and adapt to new technologies, keeping them competitive in a changing job market.
• Creating an online portfolio, starting an e-business or training other youth online showcases their abilities and work history, an effective way to attract potential employers.
• Exploring freelance options lets them find short-term, project-based or remote work, expanding their job search globally.
• Using online collaboration tools lets them work efficiently in virtual teams, a valuable skill for employers seeking team-oriented people for remote or hybrid work.
• Participating in virtual job fairs and career expos engages them directly with recruiters, revealing job openings, internships and development opportunities not found through traditional methods.
• Mastering communication for virtual interviews (Zoom/MS Teams/Skype/Google Meet) allows them to excel in online interviews and present themselves professionally in a digital job market.
• Following industry blogs, news sites and forums keeps them updated on developments and aware of the latest hiring opportunities.
• Exploring emerging fields such as artificial intelligence, data science and cybersecurity, which are popular 21st-century careers, opens doors to innovative career opportunities and improves their job prospects.
(2 x 4) (8)

subQuestions.questionText: Evaluate the significance of print media in an advancing digital world.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award FOUR marks each for TWO well-explained responses. For full marks (evaluation) a candidate must give a POSITIVE statement and qualify it, then a NEGATIVE statement and qualify it. Any TWO of:
• Printed materials can be distributed in areas without electricity or electronic media, giving print a wider reach into rural communities; but its limited physical distribution makes it hard for a bigger audience to access, unlike digital formats that can be accessed instantly from anywhere.
• Print media is considered reliable and credible due to its editing and fact-checking processes; however, online and digital resources are more favoured for their speedy, convenient and up-to-date information.
• Reading printed resources improves focus, comprehension and memory retention, especially for in-depth academic material; however, producing print harms the environment by consuming natural resources, making digital platforms a more sustainable option.
• Print media remains valuable for advertisers targeting specific audiences, as it has longer-lasting exposure; but it can be expensive to print and distribute, making it a less practical option.
• Certain print formats such as journals and magazines still attract a loyal audience due to their specialised content; whereas younger readers are turning to digital media, which has more variety and appeal suited to their fast-paced lives.
• Printed materials offer a setting free from digital interruptions like advertisements and notifications, making them ideal for deep reading and reflection; yet they cannot compete with digital platforms that provide real-time news and constant content updates.
• Books, newspapers and magazines in print can endure for generations, preserving information in an unchanging format; yet digital copies are more convenient to store, especially where physical capacity is limited.
• Owning physical books is a personalised experience because you have ownership over them; however, print materials can be expensive for some families compared with digital books, which are often cheaper, easier to access and can be shared online.
(2 x 4) (8) [20]

questions.title: SECTION C (Answer any TWO of Questions 4, 5 and 6) — Question 6: Recruitment processes (General trends and practices)
questions.passageText:
RECRUITMENT PROCESSES — General trends and practices

Current recruitment processes are driven by technology and data analytics, with a strong focus on a candidate's work experience. Therefore, choosing the right references to list in your curriculum vitae (CV) and researching a company's mission statement may be to your benefit when you are considered for a job.

[Adapted from www.hr-simplified.co.za. Accessed on 2 March 2025.]

Write paragraphs on recruitment processes using the three points below as a guideline.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly state FOUR factors to consider when adding someone as a reference in your curriculum vitae (CV).
subQuestions.memoText:
Award ONE mark for each response. Any FOUR of:
• Select individuals such as employers/supervisors/teachers who will speak or write positively about your skills, work ethic and character.
• Choose someone with a strong professional connection to you.
• Identify the person who can best give a positive, credible assessment of your abilities.
• Ensure the person has valid, professional contact details.
• Get consent/permission from the reference to use their details on your application.
• Verify that the person's details are accurate and up to date.
• Make sure the person's work experience/credentials are relevant to the job you are applying for.
• Select references with strong professional credibility and a good reputation in their field.
• Consider the reference's availability and willingness to respond promptly.
(4 x 1) (4)

subQuestions.questionText: Analyse the importance of researching a company's mission statement when applying for available jobs.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award FOUR marks each for TWO well-explained responses. For full marks a candidate must give a statement, elaborate on it, qualify it and give an outcome. Researching the mission statement may:
• Show whether the company's goals align with yours, so you can assess whether your skills and values contribute to their objectives, helping you decide which position to apply for and ensuring you end up in a job that suits your strengths and interests.
• Show the direction the company is moving in, letting you assess the potential for career growth and whether it fits your aspirations, helping you make an informed career choice.
• Give an understanding of the company's expectations, reflecting its vision and giving you a clear sense of what will be required, so you are better prepared if employed.
• Provide insight into the company's culture, helping you understand the workplace atmosphere and whether you could integrate well, increasing your chances of thriving as an employee.
• Give information about the company's reputation and position in the industry, which affects your professional reputation if appointed, protecting your career image and future prospects.
• Prepare you for an interview by giving a broad overview of the company's profile, putting you in a better position to answer questions aligned with its vision and improving your chances of securing the job.
• Indicate the company's involvement in corporate social responsibility and ethical practice, helping you choose a company that matches your moral standards and gives you job satisfaction, enhancing your well-being.
• Impress potential employers when you reference the mission statement in your application or adapt your CV, showing you are proactive, well prepared and genuinely interested, increasing your chance of a job offer.
(2 x 4) (8)

subQuestions.questionText: Evaluate why an employer may choose to hire a candidate with previous work experience.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award FOUR marks each for TWO well-explained responses. For full marks (evaluation) a candidate must give a POSITIVE statement and qualify it, then a NEGATIVE statement and qualify it. Any TWO of:
• They require less training and could start work immediately, as they already have the skills and knowledge needed; however, they may find it difficult to learn new ways of doing things and struggle to adjust to company policies.
• They have a proven track record showing reliability and work ethic; on the other hand, experience does not always mean they do the job well, as they may have bad work habits or use old-fashioned methods.
• They know the industry well and understand how the workplace functions; however, they may not bring new ideas or fresh thinking, as they may lack creativity and innovation.
• They could be good at solving problems, handling challenges and working under pressure; however, if they are too experienced they may find the job too easy and quickly lose interest or seek other opportunities.
• They show dedication and stability, as their work history shows they are responsible and can stay in a job long term; however, they may expect high salaries, better benefits or special treatment, putting strain on the company.
• They have strong people skills and know how to communicate, work in teams and manage time; yet, if they come from a very different work environment, they may struggle to fit into the new company's way of doing things, leading to conflict or misunderstandings.
• They strengthen the company's credibility and help attract clients and investors; however, an over-emphasis on experience may disadvantage other employees who have the skills but lack formal work experience.
• They are regarded as prepared for leadership roles, reducing the need to outsource candidates; whereas some may be unwilling to take on leadership responsibilities or may not be equipped to manage younger, dynamic teams.
• They can mentor and guide less experienced colleagues, improving overall team performance; but they may dominate discussions and impose their own ways of doing things, limiting innovation.
• They have a developed professional network that could benefit the company through contacts and partnerships; though over-reliance on past networks may hinder building new internal relationships, affecting cohesion.
(2 x 4) (8) [20]
